# Calvary Women's Services: Full Findings Report (All Modules)

**Audience:** consulting team  
**As of:** data 2026-10-10; text regenerated by `scripts/lib/full_findings.py` from the module readouts, the insight register, the verdict and the discoveries log (revised after the October 2026 independent review, `reports/review/`)  
**Covers:** modules M1–M10, the funding-pressure verdict, discovery flags D1–D3 and the insight register

**Purpose.** One document with every module's question, method, findings, charts, caveats and confidence, around the two anchor questions: how much funding pressure Calvary's reliance on government creates, and which other funding fits. Every chart ID maps to `chart_data/<id>.csv`; `scripts/lib/trace.py` checks the chain to the source registry.

---

## Summary of findings

One line per register finding, in module order. The module sections below carry the evidence.

**M1 Calvary financial trajectory FY2011–FY2025.** Government supplied 40%-61% of Calvary's revenue in every year FY15-FY25 on the audit basis (line 1e for FY24-25), and most of the growth since FY19. FY25 ran a $607K deficit and the cash cushion fell to 4.4 months, versus 7.5 months in FY21; about $0.42M of the $0.8M fall in reported contributions is the gala moving from line 1c to line 8a. Event receipts held near $0.5-0.6M: $596K in FY24 and $533K in FY25. The FY25 990 reported gala receipts as fundraising-event income (line 8a) instead of event contributions (line 1c); there was no collapse. Filed institutional grants to Calvary have stayed near $1M a year from 26-29 funders, and one funder (GWCF incl. the Health Equity Fund) is 27% of five-year filed grants; the top five are 63%. The FY22 revenue spike ($8.87M) was a one-time $3.68M SLFRF award for the New Foundations building, not operating growth.

**M2 government exposure and stress test.** Calvary's recurring government awards rose from about $0.6M (2020) to about $4.1M (2024) across three channels: OVSJG, HUD CoC via TCP, and DHS via TCP; about three-quarters (78% of the 2024 base) passes through TCP. In FY24-FY25 Calvary recognized only about 73%-67% of its known award ceilings as revenue. DC's budgets behind Calvary's local streams stayed flat to rising through FY2027, but the Mayor proposed cuts to victim services and DV lines in both FY2026 and FY2027 and the Council restored them. Calvary receives about 5% of DC's CoC awards and about 1% of OVSJG's awards. A non-renewed DHS/TCP contract would remove about $0.65M-$1.13M a year, depending on how recognized revenue splits across streams; the combined worst case removes $1.05M-$1.47M and leaves about 1.5-2.0 months of cash after one year even with 50% cost avoidance. Sisters Rise (24 EHV-paired PSH beds in the HIC; DHS contract capacity 25; $593K in FY2024) disappeared from the 2025 Housing Inventory Count.

**M3 peer benchmarking.** Calvary's government share (53%, FY2022-24 mean) ranks 11 of 19 DC-area organizations: below every DC DV provider (DASH 70%, My Sister's Place 83%, DC SAFE 89%) and above the philanthropy-led models (Christ House, Thrive DC, Miriam's Kitchen). Among organizations that report government revenue, Calvary's government share is near the median in DC human services and among national women's/DV organizations; against all filers (no line counted as 0%) it is in the top quarter. The peer rank (M3-01) is the stronger evidence. Calvary's real revenue growth FY19-FY24 (+13.8%/yr) trails only My Sister's Place, DWC and DC SAFE; Miriam's Kitchen grew 12% a year with almost no government money. Calvary's liquidity (5.2 months FY2024, 4.4 in FY2025) is mid-pack; government-anchored DV providers run on about one month of cash or less, while Doorways, N Street Village and Everyone Home DC hold 8-12 months. Calvary already works institutional funders harder than most peers: 42 institutional funders TY2020-24 and filed institutional grants equal to 12% of revenue, versus 8% at House of Ruth DC, 6% at N Street Village and 11% at Miriam's Kitchen; only Samaritan Inns (27%) is far ahead. Three replicable paths among peers: Samaritan Inns replaced government (72% -> 11%) with program and private revenue while holding revenue; N Street Village grew on private money at a stable ~40% share; DWC and House of Ruth MD scaled with government rising above 55%.

**M4 funder landscape (DC and DMV).** DMV funders put about $132.10M a year into DC-sector organizations TY2020-24 ($660.49M total): 58% through DAF sponsors and 42% from 555 institutional funders. The institutional pool is concentrated: the top 10 funders give 55% of institutional dollars to the DC sector, and 6 of the top 25 already fund Calvary. The typical institutional grant to a DC-sector organization is small (median $10K); six-figure grants are the top decile and come from community and private foundations. Fidelity Charitable moved $179.22M into DC-sector organizations in five years, more than any foundation; DAF money is a donor-cultivation channel, not a grant pipeline. Most institutional money to the DC sector is general operating or untagged; grants whose purpose names housing, DV or women are a minority, and the biggest mission-tagged funders are Maryland and Virginia foundations that give little in DC.

**M5 funder gap analysis.** 23 institutional funders give to three or more of Calvary's 18 peers and have no filed grant to Calvary; 75 give to two or more. 11 former institutional funders filed itemized grant lists since TY2023 with nothing for Calvary; they once gave $0.16M in total. 15 of Calvary's current institutional funders that also fund two or more peers have written larger single grants to a core peer than to Calvary. Only 44% of the CRM's $10.6M in 2023-26 institutional giving is verifiable in funders' own filings; corporate givers with no public filing (MGAC, IMF, Latham, Frontier Co-op) are $2.6M and 'see attached' filers (Philip L. Graham, Clark-Winchcole, Kay, Herb Block) $1.3M.

**M6 network analysis.** The funder web around Calvary and its peers has 328 funders; the most connected institutional funders (GWCF 18 of 19 organizations, Cafritz 14, Venable 10, Abell 9) already fund Calvary except Venable, and the DAF sponsors (Fidelity, Benevity, Schwab) connect almost everyone. Calvary shares the most institutional funders with Miriam's Kitchen (17), DASH (14) and House of Ruth DC (14); House of Ruth DC and House of Ruth MD have the longest lists of institutional funders Calvary lacks. Board interlocks are a thin channel: Calvary has 8 shared-board links in filings, none at high confidence in public filings; 8 medium-confidence links include Washington Area Women's Foundation, United Way NCA, United Way of Central Maryland and Miriam's Kitchen.

**M7 opportunity pipeline and scoring.** The scored pipeline has 182 rows: 9 Tier 1 (pursue now), 39 Tier 2, 134 Tier 3. Tier 1 institutional targets (5): William S Abell Foundation, Greater Washington Community Foundation, Morris And Gwendolyn Cafritz Foundation, John Edward Fowler Memorial Foundation, Robert I Schattner Foundation.

**M8 mission-expansion scan.** The adjacent areas Calvary already touches (DV, behavioral health, workforce, education) carry about $149.22M a year of DMV institutional grants whose purpose names them; physical health is the largest pool one step further ($84.15M/yr, 206 funders at $100K+). The Grants.gov feed yields only 36 relevant federal notices across all areas after filtering; the federal path for Calvary runs through DC intermediaries (TCP, OVSJG, DHS), not direct competition.

**M9 need and capacity context.** Calvary's service area carries the city's deepest need: Ward 8 poverty 31% and Ward 7 23% against 15% for DC; female poverty 32% in Ward 8; a third of renters in both wards pay over half their income in rent. DC's homeless count fell from 8,350 (2016) to 5,138 (2025) while Calvary's inventory grew to 124 beds across transitional, permanent supportive and rapid-rehousing programs; its 94 transitional beds are 6.8% of DC's.

**M10 named-comparator profiles (Calvary CEO request).** DWC grew from $6.31M (FY2014) to $34.40M (FY2024) while its government share rose from 24% to 57%; its federal money is 99% pass-through (HUD CoC, ESG, VOCA), the same channels Calvary uses. The SheWorks parent (CBWC Empowerment Institute, founded 2022) is 70% government at $1.84M revenue, down from 88% in its first year, with private contributions rising from $169K to $558K; SheWorks itself launched in late 2025 with labor-federation and health-plan partners, so its funding will only appear in TY2025+ filings.

## M1 Calvary financial trajectory FY2011–FY2025

Script `scripts/01_m1_trajectory.py`. Chart data `chart_data/m1_*.csv`, charts `charts/m1_*.png`. Insights M1-01 to M1-05 in `insight_register.csv`.

### Question
How has Calvary's revenue, mix, margin and liquidity moved over 15 years, and how concentrated is its private funding?

### Method
- Revenue, expenses, net assets and cash from `fact_org_financials` preferred 990 rows (one per fiscal year; five sources agree within 1%). Real values use the CPI-U deflator to 2024 dollars in `dim_period`.
- Government revenue on the **audit basis** (contracts and grants ÷ audited total revenue) for FY13–FY23, and 990 line 1e ÷ 990 revenue for FY24–FY25. Line 1e equalled the audited figure in FY22 and FY23, so the FY24–25 numbers are treated as reliable; the FY21 line 1e ($503K vs $1.98M audited) is the known exception.
- Private contributions ex-events = contributions total − government − line 1c events. The 990 does not split foundations from individuals, so institutional giving is measured separately from funders' own filings (`fact_grants`, 990-PF and Schedule I rows naming Calvary, TY2020–24, excluding cumulative rows, aggregated by funder EIN).
- Concentration: funder shares of five-year filed grants and a Herfindahl index.

### Findings

| | FY19 | FY21 | FY22 | FY23 | FY24 | FY25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenue (nominal) | $2.49M | $3.85M | $8.87M | $4.46M | $5.82M | $4.97M |
| Government (audit basis / line 1e) | $1.26M | $1.98M | $5.69M | $2.46M | $2.62M | $2.89M |
| Government share (audit ÷ audit revenue; 990 for FY24–25) | 49% | 50% | 61% | 51% | 45% | 58% |
| Surplus / deficit | +$83K | +$517K | +$4.32M | −$674K | +$507K | −$607K |
| Months of cash | 5.8 | 7.5 | 6.3 | 5.0 | 5.2 | 4.4 |

1. **Government supplied 40–61% of revenue every year since FY15 and most of the growth** (M1-01). Revenue went from $2.49M (FY19) to $4.97M (FY25) in nominal dollars, +59% after inflation ($3.05M to $4.84M in 2024 dollars). In nominal terms government revenue grew 130% over the same period and private contributions ex-events 85%; event receipts are covered in item 3.
2. **FY25 ran a $607K deficit and ended with 4.4 months of cash** (M1-02; 7.5 months in FY21). The 990's contributions total fell from $5.55M to $4.75M, but much of that fall is the change in how the gala was presented (item 3), not lost donors. Net assets ($8.1M) are mostly the building.
3. **Event receipts held near $0.53–0.60M (FY24 $596K, FY25 $533K)** (M1-03). The FY25 990 presented gala receipts as fundraising-event income (line 8a, with $259K of direct costs netted) instead of contributions (line 1c), so line 1c alone drops from $538K to $55K and net event income turns positive. The 2025 gala took place on 23 April 2025 (inside FY25) and the 2026 gala raised over $620K. Flag D3 is closed (resolved from the 990 itself).
4. **Filed institutional grants are flat (~$1M/yr from 26–29 funders) and concentrated** (M1-04): GWCF, including the Health Equity Fund, is 27% of five-year filed grants ($1.21M of $4.43M); the top five are 63%; HHI 1,168 (moderately concentrated). DAF sponsors add $1.09M over five years (Benevity, Fidelity, Schwab lead).
5. **FY22 was a capital event, not growth** (M1-05): the $3.68M SLFRF award bought the New Foundations building.

### Charts
- `m1_01_revenue_expenses` — revenue and expenses, nominal and 2024$, FY11–FY25
- `m1_02_revenue_mix` — stacked mix with government share labels, FY15–FY25
- `m1_03_gov_share_two_measures` — audit basis vs line 1e
- `m1_04_surplus_deficit` — annual surplus/deficit
- `m1_05_months_of_cash` — months of cash with a 3–6 month band
- `m1_06_event_income` — line 1c vs net event income (FY25 line 1c excludes the gala, reported on line 8a)
- `m1_07_funder_concentration` — top 12 filed funders with shares
- `m1_08_filed_grants_by_year` — institutional vs DAF by funder tax year

### Caveats
- No FY24/FY25 audits are public; those years rest on the 990. Line 1e matched audits in FY22–23.
- Funder tax years do not align with Calvary's fiscal year; TY2024 filings are partial and TY2025 mostly unfiled, so "flat" after TY2023 is partly filing lag.
- The 990 cannot separate individuals from foundations inside "private contributions ex-events"; the CRM export covers institutional gifts only and is cumulative over an unconfirmed window.

### Confidence
High on the revenue, margin and liquidity series and on government share through FY23; high on concentration of filed grants; medium on the FY24–25 government share (990 only).

## M2 government exposure and stress test

Script `scripts/02_m2_exposure.py`; parameters `config/scenarios.yaml`. Chart data `chart_data/m2_*.csv`, charts `charts/m2_*.png`. Insights M2-01 to M2-06.

### Question
Which government streams does Calvary depend on, how durable is each, what is happening to the pools behind them, and what would cuts do to revenue and cash?

### Method
- One source per stream from `fact_gov_awards`, never summed across sources: OVSJG award lists (DC FY2019–2026), HUD CoC award lists via TCP (competition years 2019–FY2025), DHS provider contracts via TCP (Council oversight responses, DC FY2024 only), audited SEFA lines for the small federal pass-throughs (EFSP, SNAP E&T). One-time money (SLFRF $3.68M, PPP $327K, HUD CPF $200K) is listed separately.
- Award ceilings aligned to Calvary's fiscal year (DC FY = Calvary FY; HUD CoC competition year t → operating year t+1; DHS FY2024 value carried forward) and compared with recognized government revenue.
- DC budget context from `supp_dc_budget_lines` (activity-level totals, approved vs actual vs Mayor's proposal) and `fact_policy_events`.
- Scenarios split FY25 recognized government revenue ($2.89M) across streams three ways and apply cuts from the config: (A) ceiling share (OVSJG 23%, CoC 41%, DHS 33%, other 2%); (B) CoC at its audited FY22–23 draw rate (38%), with DHS the residual; (C) ceiling share without Sisters Rise. Losses are reported as the range across the three splits. A floor case (OVSJG and CoC fully drawn, DHS the residual) is reported separately, not as a bound. "Net" assumes 50% of a lost stream's revenue is avoidable cost.

### Findings
1. **Three channels, two of them through one intermediary** (M2-01). Recurring awards grew from $0.6M (2020) to $4.1M (2024): OVSJG $0.37M (FY20) → $1.05M (FY26); CoC $0.24M (2019) → $1.77M (FY2025) across three projects; DHS/TCP $1.42M (FY2024: transitional housing $830K, Sisters Rise EHV $593K). TCP carries both CoC and DHS money, so about three-quarters (78% of the $4.1M 2024 award base, `m2_01`) passes through TCP. The series is quoted from 2020 because the 2019 value ($0.9M) adds two OVSJG Reach Up records ($292,000 and $368,935) that may be one award recorded twice.
2. **Ceilings exceed recognized revenue by a third** (M2-02, flag D1): FY24 ceilings $3.6M vs $2.62M recognized (73%); FY25 $4.3M vs $2.89M (67%). The gap is undrawn awards, timing, or an overstated DHS carry-forward. Calvary's FY22 and FY23 single audits already show CoC expenditure at 28% (FY22) and 58% (FY23) of the prior year's CoC award ceilings, so the gap is specific to the CoC stream and predates FY24 (the 2021 Reach Up expansion award, $1.22M reallocated to $0.42M in 2022, explains part). The next step is to reconcile CoC draw-down first, then DHS: Calvary's FY24/FY25 audits and TCP subgrant agreements are the single most useful documents Calvary could provide.
3. **Stream durability** (M2-03, judgment): OVSJG grants are annual and set in each spring's budget but have been restored every year; CoC renewals are usually protected but TCP cut Reach Up 65% in 2022. The FY2025 CoC NOFO was enjoined and FY2025 renewals were paid in full; the live cloud is the FY2026 CoC NOFO (protected renewals 60% of demand, a $1.3B transitional-housing and services set-aside, applications closed 30 September 2026, awards expected about December 2026, litigation pending). The DHS/TCP contract is the largest, least documented and most at risk, and Sisters Rise left the 2025 HIC (flag D2); HUD's 29 September 2026 notice ends the EHV program (families leased on 30 September 2026 convert to non-reissuable tenant-protection vouchers by 31 December 2026), so Sisters Rise's voucher base cannot be rebuilt.
4. **DC pools are flat to rising, with cuts proposed every spring** (M2-03): OVSJG Victim Services grants approved $45.5M (FY24) → $55.9M (FY25) → $55.4M (FY26) → $55.3M (FY27); the Mayor's FY26 proposal ($50.1M, −10.4%) was restored by the Council. The FY2027 OVSJG restoration is $5.1M one-time plus $0.5M recurring, so the FY2028 base is at risk again. DHS continuum $170M (FY24) → $206M (FY26) → $194M (FY27); PSH $145–166M. Actual spending runs 9–14% below approved on OVSJG.
5. **Calvary is a price-taker** (M2-04): 5.3% of DC CoC awards, 1.1% of OVSJG awards.
6. **Scenarios** (M2-05, FY25 baseline: revenue $4.97M, expenses $5.58M, cash $2.06M, deficit −$607K):

| Scenario | Revenue loss (range across three splits) | % of revenue | Deficit (gross) | Months of cash after a year (net) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OVSJG −10% | −$67K to −$100K | 1–2% | −$675K to −$707K | 3.0–3.1 |
| OVSJG −25% | −$168K to −$250K | 3–5% | −$776K to −$857K | 2.9–3.0 |
| CoC renewals −15% | −$99K to −$207K | 2–4% | −$707K to −$814K | 2.9–3.0 |
| One CoC project lost (New Foundations 2) | −$204K to −$424K | 4–9% | −$811K to −$1.03M | 2.7–2.9 |
| DHS/TCP contract not renewed | −$0.65M to −$1.13M | 13–23% | −$1.26M to −$1.73M | 1.9–2.4 |
| Combined (OVSJG −25%, CoC −15%, DHS lost) | −$1.05M to −$1.47M | 21–30% | −$1.66M to −$2.08M | 1.5–2.0 |

The DHS figure depends on how revenue splits across streams; the floor case with OVSJG and CoC fully drawn nearly removes it ($26K). The headline stands: the TCP channel is the cloud, since CoC and DHS together are $1.8–2.2M under every split. The headline OVSJG cuts are survivable; a TCP contract loss is not without new money or cost cuts. Even the baseline burns cash: at the FY25 run-rate, cash lasts about 41 months.

### Charts
`m2_01_stream_map`, `m2_02_ceilings_vs_recognized`, `m2_04_dc_budget_context`, `m2_05_pool_shares`, `m2_06_policy_timeline`, `m2_07_scenarios`; tables `m2_03_stream_durability.csv`, `m2_07_scenario_parameters.csv`.

### Caveats
- DHS/TCP amounts are public for FY2024 only; every other year of that stream is unknown, not zero. TCP is a pass-through intermediary with no itemized Schedule I list in the data, so TCP agreements are the only route to FY25–26 DHS values.
- HUD CoC award years are competition years; the one-year lag to Calvary's operating year is an assumption (config).
- Scenario stream shares are apportioned three ways from ceilings and the audited CoC draw rate, not from Calvary's ledger; the ledger would turn each range into one figure.
- Federal policy risk (FY2026 CoC NOFO, the EHV program's end) is only partly captured in the data and is noted as external context, dated October 2026.

### Confidence
High on the stream map, pool shares and DC budget lines; medium on ceilings-vs-recognized and the scenarios (apportionment and carry-forward assumptions); durability ratings are judgment.

## M3 peer benchmarking

Script `scripts/03_m3_peers.py`. Benchmark table `chart_data/m3_00_benchmark_table.csv`; charts `charts/m3_*.png`. Insights M3-01 to M3-06. Core peers are the 18 **provisional** organizations in `calvary_funding_data/config/core_peers.csv`; DWC and the CBWC Empowerment Institute (SheWorks) appear as Los Angeles reference rows on every chart.

### Question
Where does Calvary sit against comparable organizations on government dependence, size, growth, liquidity and private funder base, and which peers show a workable path to lower exposure?

### Method
- Preferred 990 rows from `fact_org_financials` FY2015–FY2025. Government share = line 1e ÷ total revenue, except Calvary FY≤2023 where the audit basis is used (line 1e understated FY21). Three-year means (FY2022–24) smooth single-year reporting breaks (e.g., Coalition for the Homeless FY23, Samaritan Inns FY24).
- Real growth = CAGR of 2024-dollar revenue FY2019→FY2024 (endpoints avoid Calvary's one-time FY22 award).
- Months of cash = cash and savings ÷ monthly expenses (clean-table field).
- Funder base = 990-PF/Schedule I rows naming each organization TY2020–24 (non-cumulative), split institutional vs DAF via `dim_funder.funder_type`; depth = institutional dollars ÷ FY2020–24 revenue. DMV funders' filings only, so the LA comparators' local funders are not captured. Two Baltimore funders' grants to a Baltimore namesake of My Sister's Place ($131,906) are excluded (`config/grant_exclusions.csv`).
- Resilience typology: government-anchored ≥65%, mixed 35–65%, philanthropy-led <35%.
- Sector distributions: `dc_sector` FY2023, `size_matched` FY2022, `national_women` FY2022, chosen for filing coverage. Percentiles are computed among organizations whose 990 reports a government line (n=163/334/542), and again against all filers with no government line counted as 0% (n=426/556/1,124).

### Findings

| Organization | Rev FY24 | Gov share FY22–24 | Real CAGR FY19–24 | Months of cash FY24 | Institutional funders | Inst. $ ÷ revenue | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Calvary** | $5.8M | 53% | +13.8% | 5.2 | 42 | 12% | mixed |
| DC SAFE | $7.0M | 89% | +17.7% | 0.9 | 7 | 3% | gov-anchored |
| My Sister's Place | $7.2M | 83% | +19.4% | 2.9 | 23 | 7% | gov-anchored |
| DASH | $7.0M | 70% | −2.7% | 4.0 | 23 | 5% | gov-anchored |
| House of Ruth DC | $14.6M | 53% | +5.0% | 3.8 | 83 | 8% | mixed |
| N Street Village | $10.0M | 42% | −1.7% | 8.0 | 54 | 6% | mixed |
| Samaritan Inns | $7.1M | 44% | +10.1% | 4.5 | 14 | 27% | mixed |
| Miriam's Kitchen | $11.3M | 0% | +12.0% | 4.1 | 66 | 11% | philanthropy-led |
| DWC (LA, ref.) | $34.4M | 57% | +19.0% | 2.4 | n/a | n/a | mixed |
| CBWC Inst./SheWorks (LA, ref.) | $1.5M | 86% | n/a | 4.8 | n/a | n/a | gov-anchored |

Full table: `m3_00_benchmark_table.csv` (21 organizations, all metrics).

1. **Calvary is mid-pack on government share** (M3-01): 53%, 11th of 19 DC-area organizations, below every DC DV provider (70–89%) and above the philanthropy-led models (Miriam's Kitchen, Thrive DC, Christ House). The peer rank is the stronger evidence that Calvary's share is typical. Against the broader sector (M3-02), Calvary is at the 57th percentile among DC human-services organizations that report government revenue (46th among national women's/DV organizations); against all filers, with no government line counted as 0%, it is in the top quarter (84th in DC, 74th nationally).
2. **Growth has come on both models** (M3-03): Calvary's +13.8%/yr real growth trails only My Sister's Place, DWC and DC SAFE; Miriam's Kitchen grew +12%/yr with almost no government money.
3. **Liquidity is mid-pack** (M3-04): 5.2 months in FY24 (4.4 in FY25). Government-anchored DV providers run on ~1 month; Doorways, Everyone Home DC and N Street Village hold 8–12 months.
4. **Calvary already works institutional funders harder than most peers** (M3-05): 42 institutional funders and filed institutional grants equal to 12% of revenue, versus 6–8% at N Street Village and House of Ruth DC; only Samaritan Inns (27%) is far ahead. The headroom is in grant size and multi-year commitments, in DAF/major-donor giving (N Street Village 51% of filed grants via DAFs, Calvary 25%), and in earned revenue.
5. **Three paths** (M3-06): Samaritan Inns replaced government (72% → 11%) with program-service and other revenue while revenue held near $6–7M; N Street Village grew private giving alongside a stable ~40% government share; DWC and House of Ruth MD scaled with government rising above 55%. The N Street Village path is the closest fit for Calvary; Samaritan Inns shows the earned-revenue option; DWC shows that scaling with government needs a much larger balance sheet (DWC's months of cash: 2.4).
6. **In the shared DC pools** (m3_09): the DV peers draw $3–5M a year each from OVSJG; Calvary's $1.05M makes it a mid-sized OVSJG grantee and one of the larger CoC sub-recipients ($1.77M; only Christ House and My Sister's Place draw more).

### Charts
`m3_01_gov_share_ranked`, `m3_02_size_vs_gov_share`, `m3_03_real_growth`, `m3_04_months_of_cash`, `m3_05_gov_share_trajectories` (20 small multiples), `m3_06_institutional_base`, `m3_07_sector_distributions`, `m3_08_case_studies_mix`, `m3_09_peer_pools`.

### Caveats
- Core peers are provisional; swapping them is a config edit plus rerun. Swapping three provisional peers for alternates moves Calvary from 11th to 12th of 19; confirm the peer set with Calvary before outreach.
- Line 1e understates government for organizations that book contracts as program revenue (Samaritan Inns' FY24–25 drop may be partly reclassification; its program-service revenue rose at the same time).
- Funder-base metrics cover DMV funders' filings only; TY2024 partial.
- Named comparators: DWC's fiscal year is the calendar year; CBWC Institute has three years of filings and SheWorks itself begins after TY2024.

### Confidence
High for shares, growth, liquidity and sector percentiles (on the stated comparison set); medium for funder-base depth and the typology of diversifiers (judgment on three cases).

## M4 funder landscape (DC and DMV)

Script `scripts/04_m4_landscape.py`. Landscape table `chart_data/m4_00_funder_landscape_table.csv`; charts `charts/m4_*.png`. Insights M4-01 to M4-05.

### Question
Who funds Calvary's space in DC and the DMV, at what scale, how concentrated is it, and how has it moved TY2020–24?

### Method
- Base: `fact_grants` rows from funders' own filings (990-PF grants paid, Schedule I), TY2020–24, non-cumulative, excluding two funders listed in `config/landscape_exclusions.csv` (the Gates Foundation, whose DC recipients are global-development and research organizations and which is in the data only because it appears in Calvary's CRM; and TCP, a pass-through intermediary for public funds).
- Lens A: grants to the 1,027 `dc_sector` organizations (DC public charities in homelessness, housing, DV, human services and adjacent NTEE codes). Lens B: grants to DC/MD/VA recipients whose purpose text is tagged housing, DV or women.
- Funder types from `dim_funder`; DAF sponsors (Fidelity, Schwab, Benevity/AOGF, NPT, Vanguard…) are donor intermediaries and are reported separately from institutional decision-makers.
- Institutional landscape table: one row per institutional funder with dollars, recipients, years active, median/p75/max grant, mission-tagged dollars, whether it funds Calvary, number of core peers funded, "see attached" years, and DMV/DC share of all its giving.

### Findings
1. **Scale** (M4-01): about $132M a year flows from DMV funders into DC-sector organizations ($660M TY2020–24), 58% of it through DAF sponsors and 42% ($276M) from 555 institutional funders. Institutional dollars to the sector ran $50–52M a year in TY2020–23 and $72M in TY2024 even with partial TY2024 filings.
2. **Concentration** (M4-02): the top 10 institutional funders give about half of institutional dollars to the DC sector. Of the 25 largest, 6 already fund Calvary (GWCF, Cafritz, Bank of America, United Way NCA, Jane Bancroft Robinson, Abell). The largest non-funder in TY2020–24 was Clark Charitable ($32.8M to 20 DC organizations, $7.8M of it to five core peers); those grants were a spend-down, historic and now closed (its own FAQ says it was sunsetting and operational until 31 December 2025, and it takes no unsolicited proposals). The other large non-funders are JPMorgan Chase Foundation ($18.0M, mostly matching gifts), Wal-Mart, Annie E. Casey, Weinberg, Morningstar, Diana Davis Spencer, Meyer, Capital Area Food Bank, Wells Fargo, Bernstein, The Washington Home, Schattner, Cohen.
3. **Grant size** (M4-03): the median institutional grant to a DC-sector organization is ~$15K (private foundations $10K, community foundations $40K); six-figure grants are the top decile. A $0.5M/yr increase in institutional revenue is a handful of six-figure, multi-year relationships, not dozens of $10K grants.
4. **DAF channel** (M4-04): Fidelity Charitable moved $179M into DC-sector organizations in five years, NPT $80M, Benevity $49M, Schwab $36M. This is individual-donor money routed through sponsors; Calvary's $1.1M over five years (25% of its filed grants) tracks its major donors.
5. **Purpose** (M4-05): most institutional money is general operating or untagged; dollars whose purpose names housing, DV or women are a minority. The biggest mission-tagged funders in the DMV (Weinberg, The Community Foundation, the now-closed Clark, Wells Fargo, Abell) are mostly Maryland and Virginia foundations, several of which give little in DC.

### Charts
`m4_01_dc_sector_by_year`, `m4_03_top_institutional_funders`, `m4_04_concentration`, `m4_05_grant_size_by_type`, `m4_06_daf_sponsors`, `m4_07_purpose_tags`, `m4_08_mission_tagged_funders`; tables `m4_00_funder_landscape_table.csv`, `m4_02_dc_sector_by_funder_type.csv`.

### Caveats
- Funder tax years; TY2024 partial, TY2025 excluded.
- Clark's spend-down ($32.8M to DC's sector) inflates the TY2020–24 landscape totals; historic, now closed.
- "See attached" filers (476 returns / 667 rows, ~$3.5B DMV-wide) have no recipient names, so a few large DC funders (Philip L. Graham, Clark-Winchcole, Bank of America in some years) are under-counted.
- Corporate giving without a foundation vehicle is invisible here (it appears only in Calvary's CRM and peers' donor lists).
- The sector universe includes DC-based national organizations; Gates is excluded for this reason, and a few other research-oriented recipients remain.

### Confidence
High on totals, concentration and grant sizes; medium on purpose tags (keyword-based) and on the mission-tagged lens.

## M5 funder gap analysis

Script `scripts/05_m5_gaps.py`. Candidate base `chart_data/m5_00_candidate_funders.csv` (166 funders with evidence fields; input to M7 scoring); charts `charts/m5_*.png`. Insights M5-01 to M5-04.

### Question
Which funders support Calvary's peers or the DC sector but not Calvary, which former funders have lapsed, where do current funders have headroom, and how much of Calvary's CRM-recorded institutional giving can be verified?

### Method
- Filed grants (990-PF, Schedule I) TY2020–24, non-cumulative, landscape exclusions applied. "Funds Calvary" = any filed grant naming Calvary TY2020–24. "Itemized TY2023+" = the funder filed itemized grant lists in TY2023 or TY2024, so the absence of a Calvary grant is current, not filing lag. "See attached" filers are flagged.
- Gap categories: (G1) institutional funders of ≥2 core peers with no Calvary grant; (G2) lapsed Calvary funders (last grant ≤TY2022, funder itemized since); (G3) current funders whose largest grant to a core peer exceeds their largest to Calvary; (G4) institutional funders giving ≥$500K to the DC sector with no Calvary grant; (G5) funders on ≥2 peer donor lists (web) but on no Calvary list or filing; plus the CRM reconciliation from `supp_crm_cash_verification`.

### Findings
1. **Peer funders not funding Calvary** (M5-01): 23 institutional funders give to three or more of the 18 peers with no filed grant to Calvary; 75 give to two or more. Of the 23, six are channels rather than grantmakers: Gifts for the Homeless (8 peers; in-kind), T. Rowe Price Program for Charitable Giving (8; a DAF-like program), Capital Area Food Bank (7; in-kind food), America's Charities (7; workplace giving, also in the CRM), JPMorgan Chase Foundation (7; matching gifts) and Give Lively (online giving). Clark Charitable Foundation (5 peers, $7.8M, median grant $250K) has closed, and Venable Foundation (10 peers; in Calvary's CRM for $75K) is closed to new applicants (Calvary qualifies only if its recent gifts came from the Foundation rather than the firm). The other 15 choose their own grantees. Funders of four or more peers: Schattner (4, $800K, typical grant $60K; Tier 1), Bunting (4, $120K, typical $10K) and Bechtel (4, $100K, typical $25K); the last two give little elsewhere in DC, publish no application process and sit in Tier 3. The three-peer names, Cohen (3, $940K; also invitation-only), Bernstein (3, $908K), The Washington Home (3, $873K), Dweck, Jack R. Anderson, Collins and six others, depend on the provisional peer set. 22 of the 23 filed itemized lists in TY2023+.
2. **Lapsed funders** (M5-02): 11 former institutional funders itemized grants since TY2023 with nothing for Calvary; they once gave $0.16M ($156,150): Many Hands ($55.5K, TY2020), Jane Bancroft Robinson ($25K, TY2020), Robert M. Fisher ($25K, TY2022), Junior League of Washington, Levatus, Phase Foundation, Poole, Spur Local, Jacquemin, Grossman, Whispering Bells. Many Hands requires an operating budget of $500K–$5M; Calvary spent $5.58M in FY2025, so it is not eligible for the January 2027 cycle unless both FY2026 actual expenses and the FY2027 budget fall to $5M. World Bank Community Connections Fund is not lapsed: its one filed grant to Calvary was a one-time $100K capital-campaign grant (TY2022), and staff giving through the fund continued to July 2026 in Calvary's records, so it is an employee-giving channel. Max & Victoria Dreyfus is unclear (no itemized TY2023+ return in the data).
3. **Headroom with current funders** (M5-03): among current funders that also fund two or more peers, 15 have written larger single grants to a core peer than to Calvary. The material ones: Cafritz ($170K to Calvary vs $250K to a peer), GWCF ($458K vs $526K; Calvary's grant is Health Equity Fund money and the peer grant is also fund-specific), Bank of America ($15K vs $50K), United Way NCA ($23K vs $56K), Ludwig ($25K vs $50K), Shaver, Fowler ($40K vs $50K), Dreyfus.
4. **DC-sector majors without Calvary** (G4): 65 institutional funders gave ≥$500K to DC-sector organizations TY2020–24 with no Calvary grant (41 of them appear on no other gap list), led by Clark (historic spend-down, now closed), JPMorgan Chase, Wal-Mart, Casey, Weinberg, Morningstar, Diana Davis Spencer, Rast, Meyer, Capital Area Food Bank, Wells Fargo ("see attached" since TY2023), Bernstein, PepsiCo, The Washington Home, ImpactAssets, Public Welfare, Coca-Cola, Schattner, Bainum, Cohen.
5. **Web-list-only gaps** (G5): 16 names appear on two or more peer donor lists but on no Calvary list or filing, mostly corporations with no public filing (Accenture, Boeing, Carlyle, Deloitte, GMMB, Mars Foundation, World Bank Group) plus Helen Bechtel Foundation, Alexander & Margaret Stewart Trust, Lenzner Family Foundation, Capitol Hill Community Foundation, Green Charitable Foundation.
6. **CRM reconciliation** (M5-04): of the CRM's $10.56M (160 funders, 2023–26), $4.63M (44%, 25 funders) is confirmed in the funder's own TY2023+ filing; $2.55M (92 funders) is corporate or otherwise has no public filing (MGAC, IMF, Latham & Watkins, Frontier Co-op, Reservoir); $1.61M (29 exempt filers) shows no Calvary row; $1.28M comes from "see attached" filers (Philip L. Graham, Clark-Winchcole, Kay, Herb Block, Loughran, Kirkland & Ellis); $0.48M was confirmed only in earlier years.

### Charts
`m5_01_peer_funders_not_calvary`, `m5_02_lapsed_funders`, `m5_03_current_funder_headroom`, `m5_06_crm_reconciliation`; tables `m5_04_dc_majors_not_calvary.csv`, `m5_05_web_list_gaps.csv`, `m5_00_candidate_funders.csv`.

### Caveats
- A "gap" in filings can be a gift routed through a DAF, a corporate matching program or a fiscal sponsor; check the CRM before outreach.
- Peer donor lists are undated and amount-less, and only six peers publish them.
- Several high-count gap funders are channels (in-kind, workplace, matching-gift, online and employee giving) rather than grantmakers; M7 labels them as channels and caps them at Tier 2.
- Clark's TY2020–24 grants were a spend-down; historic and now closed, they inflate the gap totals.
- Core peers are provisional; the gap list moves if the peer set changes. Swapping three provisional peers drops Cohen, Bernstein and The Washington Home from the three-peer list, so confirm the peer set with Calvary before outreach.

### Confidence
High on the filing-based gap and lapsed lists; medium on headroom (single largest grants may be capital or restricted) and on web-list gaps.

## M6 network analysis

Script `scripts/06_m6_network.py`. Tables `chart_data/m6_01_central_funders.csv`, `m6_04_board_interlocks.csv`, `m6_05_relationship_paths.csv`; charts `charts/m6_02_cofunding_overlap.png`, `m6_03_network.png`. Insights M6-01 to M6-03.

### Question
Which funders sit at the center of the web around Calvary and its peers, which peers share Calvary's funders, how much do board interlocks add, and how strong is the relationship path to each candidate funder?

### Method
- Bipartite graph: funders × 19 recipients (Calvary + 18 provisional peers), edges = filed grants TY2020–24 (990-PF, Schedule I; landscape exclusions applied). Degree = organizations funded; betweenness on the unweighted graph.
- Co-funding overlap per peer: shared institutional funders with Calvary (DAF sponsors excluded), Jaccard, and the peer's institutional funders that do not fund Calvary.
- Board interlocks from `fact_org_relationships` (`shared_board_member`), restricted to links touching Calvary, a peer or a named comparator. Person records are matched in Prompt 1 only on an exact normalized name plus a corroborating signal. A link stays high only when the two board tenures overlap (a name match across terms that never overlap is medium), and the other organization counts as a funder only if it has at least one filed grant (universe membership alone is not enough). **Leadership materials use high-confidence links only; medium links are labeled "unconfirmed" and go to the consulting team.** No names are stored in the analysis outputs (person_id only).
- Relationship-path score per candidate funder (0–1): 0.40 × peers funded (cap 12) + 0.25 × close peers funded (peers sharing ≥5 institutional funders with Calvary; cap 8) + 0.25 × Calvary's current institutional funders whose grantee sets overlap the candidate's by ≥2 (cap 20) + 0.10 × any high-confidence board link. Consulting variant adds 0.05 for a medium link.

### Findings
1. **Central funders** (M6-01): 328 funders connect the 19 organizations. By organizations funded: Fidelity 18, GWCF 18, Benevity/AOGF 18, Schwab DAF 16, Cafritz 14, Vanguard 13, NPT 13, United Way NCA 13, Blackbaud Giving Fund 11, Venable Foundation 10, Bank of America 10, Abell 9, T. Rowe Price Program 8, Fowler 8, Gifts for the Homeless 8. Every one of these funds Calvary except Venable, T. Rowe Price, Gifts for the Homeless and (further down) Capital Area Food Bank, America's Charities, JPMorgan Chase and Clark (now closed). Calvary is in the core of the web, not at its edge.
2. **Overlap** (M6-02): Calvary shares the most institutional funders with Miriam's Kitchen (17), DASH (14), House of Ruth DC (14), New Endeavors by Women (12) and My Sister's Place (12). The longest lists of institutional funders Calvary lacks belong to House of Ruth MD (81), House of Ruth DC (69), Miriam's Kitchen (48), N Street Village (45), Community of Hope (33), Doorways (29).
3. **Board interlocks are thin** (M6-03): Calvary has no high-confidence board links in public filings. Its 8 shared-board links are all medium confidence and unconfirmed (Washington Area Women's Foundation, United Way NCA, United Way of Central Maryland, DAVIS Construction Foundation, Charter School Incubator Initiative, Miriam's Kitchen, Dress for Success, Clean Power Institute). The Clean Power Institute link, once labelled high, spans board terms that never overlap, and that organization has no filed grants, so it is not a funder. Across all 19 organizations, 28 interlocks touch a funder, none at high confidence. Paths run through shared funders and peers, not boards. `candidate_interlocks` (low confidence) has one row touching the peer set and none touching Calvary. The 17 board-employer overlaps noted in Prompt 1 (Capital One, DAVIS, Venable, KPMG, Baker Tilly…) come from annual-report board lists and are a stronger lead than filings, but they are corporate relationships, not foundation boards.
4. **Paths** (m6_05): the strongest paths to non-funders run through peers: Venable (10 peers, 9 close, 22 overlapping co-funders), T. Rowe Price Program (8/7/16), JPMorgan Chase (7/7/15), Capital Area Food Bank, America's Charities, Clark (5/5/14; closed), Give Lively, Schattner, Bunting, Bechtel. Several of these are channels or closed to new applicants (M5, M7). Among current funders the deepest embedded are GWCF, Cafritz, Abell, Fowler, Bank of America and United Way NCA.

### Charts and tables
`m6_02_cofunding_overlap`, `m6_03_network` (58 funders of 3+ organizations; PNG), `m6_01_central_funders.csv`, `m6_03_network_nodes.csv`, `m6_04_board_interlocks.csv`, `m6_05_relationship_paths.csv`.

### Caveats
- The graph covers DMV funders' filings; corporate giving and DAF-routed individual gifts are only partly visible.
- Interlocks depend on name matching; a medium-confidence match may be two different people. Treat as leads.
- Path weights are analyst choices (documented in the manifest note); M7 lets them be reweighted.

### Confidence
High on the graph and overlap counts; high that board paths are thin; medium on the path-strength construct.

## M7 opportunity pipeline and scoring

Script `scripts/07_m7_pipeline.py`; weights and tier cutoffs in `config/scoring_weights.yaml`. Outputs `recommendations/funder_pipeline.csv` (also `chart_data/m7_00_funder_pipeline.csv`) and `recommendations/action_plan_90day.csv`; charts `m7_02_pipeline_scores`, `m7_03_tier1_score_breakdown`. Insight M7-01.

### Question
Which funders and programs should Calvary pursue first, and on what evidence?

### Method
Candidate base = M5 (current funders with headroom, lapsed funders, peer-funder gaps, DC-sector majors) joined to M6 relationship paths and the M4 landscape. DAF sponsors are excluded (a channel, not a grantmaker); the T. Rowe Price Program is scored like a DAF. Current funders that gave Calvary under $10K over TY2020–24 are dropped before scoring. Seven dimensions scored 0–1, weighted (mission fit 0.20, peer giving 0.20, regional giving 0.10, award size 0.15, accessibility 0.10, durability 0.10, relationship 0.15):

| Dimension | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Mission fit | funder issue tags (housing/DV/women = 1.0; behavioral health/workforce/health 0.7; general operating 0.6) plus the share of its DC-sector dollars whose purpose names housing/DV/women |
| Peer giving | core peers funded TY2020–24, capped at 8 |
| Regional giving | dollars to DC-sector organizations, log scale $50K → $10M |
| Award size | median grant to peers (else median DC-sector grant, then Calvary's largest grant), log scale $5K → $250K |
| Accessibility | funder type and breadth (community foundation 0.85; public charity grantmaker 0.75; private foundation 0.70 / 0.50 / 0.30 by number of DC recipients); −0.15 for "see attached" filers; −0.30 for in-kind or workplace-giving channels |
| Durability | years funding peers and years active in the DC sector |
| Relationship | M6 path strength + 0.35 current funder + 0.20 lapsed + 0.15 on Calvary's CRM/lists |

Tiers: **Tier 1** score ≥ 0.62 and typical grant ≥ $25K (max 20); **Tier 2** score ≥ 0.48; **Tier 3** the rest. Channels (DAF-like, workplace, matching-gift, in-kind, online and employee giving) and funders closed to new applicants are capped at Tier 2; closed funders are kept in the file for the record (Tier 3, track "excluded: closed funder"), never as prospects; funders Calvary is not eligible for sit in Tier 3 with the reason. Status comes from `open_status` in `config/guideline_notes.csv`, checked on each funder's own page (October 2026). These rules are documented in `config/scoring_weights.yaml`. Government rows (OVSJG, DHS/TCP, HUD CoC, DHS PSH, HUD CPF) and corporate CRM relationships (≥$50K, no public filing) carry analyst scores (basis = inferred). Federal Grants.gov notices are Tier 3 by default.

### Result (182 rows; Tier 1 = 9, Tier 2 = 39, Tier 3 = 134)
| Track | Tier 1 | Tier 2 | Tier 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Institutional: steward / upgrade | 4 (Abell, GWCF, Cafritz, Fowler) | 9 | 22 |
| Institutional: new | 1 (Schattner) | 10 (The Washington Home, Cohen, Viragh, Arlington CF, Coca-Cola, Morrison & Foerster, Eugene B. Casey, ImpactAssets; Venable and Meyer, closed to new applicants) | 97 |
| Channels | – | 8 (T. Rowe Price Program, donor-advised; America's Charities, workplace giving; JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, matching gifts with a corporate-relationship path; Gifts for the Homeless and Capital Area Food Bank, in-kind; Give Lively, online giving; World Bank CCF, employee giving) | – |
| Closed or not eligible | – | – | 3 (Clark, closed; Weinberg and Many Hands, not eligible) |
| Corporate (CRM) | 1 (MGAC) | 10 (Frontier Co-op, IMF, Reservoir, Latham & Watkins, UnitedHealth, …) | – |
| Government DC | 2 (OVSJG grants; DHS/TCP contracts) | 1 (DHS PSH expansion) | – |
| Government federal | 1 (HUD CoC via TCP) | 1 (HUD CPF renewal) | 12 opportunities |

**Tier 1 (9 rows):** five foundations, three government streams and one corporate partner: Abell (0.86), GWCF (0.85), OVSJG (0.80), Cafritz (0.78), HUD CoC via TCP (0.78), DHS/TCP (0.72), Fowler (0.72), MGAC (0.70, corporate), Schattner (0.67). Clark Charitable Foundation (the A. James & Alice B. Clark Foundation) would score 0.82 but has closed: its own FAQ says it was sunsetting and operational until 31 December 2025, and it takes no unsolicited proposals. America's Charities is a workplace-giving federation already paying Calvary, not a grantmaker, so it sits in Tier 2 as a channel. The T. Rowe Price Program is capped at Tier 2 as a donor-advised channel and Frontier Co-op falls to Tier 2 under the score cutoff.

**90-day plan** (`action_plan_90day.csv`): sequenced for a fundraising team Calvary held at six positions with limited growth over 2021–24 (Calvary's 2021–24 strategic plan report; internal, Calvary-facing use only). Month 1, government confirmations by day 30 (FY26 award letters, draw-down against ceilings with CoC reconciled first, FY27 renewal calendar), owned by the CEO and board chair. Month 2, two current-funder conversations a fortnight (development director): Abell, steward and renew (largest grant $270K in TY2021, latest filed $25K in TY2023, a further $25K in March 2025 in Calvary's records; invitation-only with no consecutive-year requests, so ask its staff when a next request is welcome and what it would fund); GWCF, a successor to the Health Equity Fund support behind its $458K plus a core general-operating request; Cafritz ($170K vs $250K largest to a peer) and Fowler ($40K vs $50K), a multi-year general-operating grant at the funder's peer-level amount; MGAC, cash vs in-kind. Month 3, introductions: Schattner is invitation-only, so the step is to secure an invitation through a named peer or co-funder (no LOI). Tier 2 channel step: confirm Calvary's enrollment in the CFC and employer campaigns and its designation code (America's Charities). Small check: confirm the FY26 gala date. Owner roles: CEO + board chair for ≥$100K and government rows; development director otherwise.

### Caveats
- Scores rank evidence, not fit with funder guidelines; the approved web pull on Tier 1–2 guidelines and deadlines is merged into the pipeline (`application_process`, `next_deadline_or_cycle`, `guidelines_url`, `guidelines_basis`, `open_status`; notes in `config/guideline_notes.csv`).
- High-count gap funders that are channels are labelled as channels and capped at Tier 2 (penalized, not removed); Clark is kept for the record only.
- Leadership materials name a funder only after its open status is checked on its own page. Invitation-only funders get an introduction through a named peer or co-funder that leads to an invitation (Schattner, Cohen), or a question to staff where Calvary is a current grantee (Abell); never an LOI.
- Three-peer names (The Washington Home, Cohen) depend on the provisional peer set (`peer_set_note`).
- Government and corporate scores are analyst judgment.
- Weights are editable; rerun `07_m7_pipeline.py` after changing `config/scoring_weights.yaml`.

### Confidence
Medium: the ordering is robust to moderate weight changes (9 or 10 of the top ten institutional rows stay in the top ten under ±0.05 changes, `m7_05_sensitivity`); exact ranks are not.

## M8 mission-expansion scan

Script `scripts/08_m8_expansion.py`; area definitions and distance ratings in `config/expansion_areas.yaml`. Tables `chart_data/m8_01_expansion_scan.csv`, `m8_02_federal_opportunities.csv`; chart `m8_01_expansion_scan`. Insights M8-01, M8-02.

### Question
Which funding pools open up if Calvary formalizes or adds adjacent programs, and how far is each from current operations?

### Method
For each program area in `dim_program_area`: DMV institutional grant dollars TY2020–24 whose purpose text carries the tag (DAF sponsors and landscape exclusions removed), funders active and funders at $100K+, median grant, federal Grants.gov notices after removing research, tribal, rural and overseas notices and keeping relevant agencies (HUD, VA, DOL, DOJ, ACF, SAMHSA, USDA, Treasury, ACL), DC policy events, and an analyst distance rating: core, near (already delivered in some form), medium (same clients, new capability or credential), far (new population or licensing).

### Findings
| Area | Distance | DMV $/yr (tagged) | Funders ($100K+) | Federal notices | Calvary today | Models |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Housing and homelessness | core | $32.4M | 391 (104) | 9 | TH 94, PSH 16, RRH 14 | N Street Village, DWC |
| Education and life skills | near | $93.7M | 744 (271) | 5 | LEAP | N Street Village, Thrive DC |
| Workforce and employment | near | $30.4M | 181 (66) | 6 | Step Up DC; SNAP E&T | SheWorks (stipends, childcare, employer partners); DWC MADE |
| Behavioral health and recovery | near | $20.7M | 251 (84) | 17 | On-site therapy, recovery | Samaritan Inns; N Street Village |
| DV and victim services | near | $4.5M | 161 (34) | 3 | DV-designated site; OVSJG | DASH, My Sister's Place, DC SAFE |
| Physical health | medium | $84.2M | 697 (206) | 0 | Meals, partnerships | Community of Hope (FQHC), Christ House, DWC clinic |
| Aging and older adults | medium | $9.7M | 153 (34) | 2 | Older PSH residents | DWC; The Washington Home |
| Women veterans | medium | $7.7M | 152 (34) | 5 | None documented | Access Housing DC; VA GPD |
| Reentry | medium | $1.0M | 39 (8) | 5 | Served, not named | SheWorks; OVSJG reentry |
| Maternal and family health | far | $4.2M | 60 (12) | 3 | Single women only | Community of Hope, House of Ruth |

1. **Near pools are substantial** (M8-01): education, workforce, behavioral health and DV together carry about $149M a year of tagged DMV institutional grants. Calvary already runs programs in each; formalizing them (named program, outcomes, credentials) opens funders without changing the mission. The education figure is dominated by schools and scholarships, so its practical share for Calvary is small; workforce and behavioral health are the real near pools.
2. **Health is the largest medium-distance pool** ($84M/yr, 206 funders at $100K+). The peer models are partnerships (DWC's clinic with JWCH; Community of Hope's FQHC), not building a clinic. A behavioral-health certification that allows Medicaid billing would turn therapy from a cost into program-service revenue (Samaritan Inns' path).
3. **Aging, veterans and reentry pools are small** in DMV philanthropy; their money is federal (VA GPD, DOL HVRP, DOJ reentry) and program-specific. Reentry fits Calvary's population (OVSJG runs reentry grants) but the private pool is $1M/yr.
4. **Federal direct competition is thin** (M8-02): 36 relevant notices in the feed, mostly HUD programs that flow through DC (ROSS, CDBG, housing counseling), DOJ BJA/OJJDP behavioral-health and reentry, SAMHSA forecasts, DOL VETS HVRP (includes homeless women veterans), VA grants. Realistic direct federal targets: HUD CPF earmark renewal, DOL HVRP (if a veterans track is added), SAMHSA treatment/recovery (with a licensed partner).

### Trade-offs for the recommendations
- **Workforce (near, recommended):** SheWorks-style cohort model inside Step Up DC; unlocks DOES/WIOA and workforce funders; outcomes are easy to show. The first cost is funding Calvary's second workforce position, which is unfunded in FY2026 (Calvary's 2021–24 strategic plan report; internal, Calvary-facing use only); beyond that, modest cost.
- **Behavioral health (near, recommended with a credential decision):** DBH certification or a partner agreement converts therapy to billable revenue; staffing and compliance cost; the biggest earned-revenue lever.
- **DV formalization (near):** Calvary already holds a DV-designated site; a formal DV program and VOCA eligibility deepen the OVSJG relationship and open DV funders (DC SAFE, DASH pattern) but add reporting burden.
- **Health partnership (medium):** on-site clinic hours with an FQHC (Community of Hope is a peer and Ward 8 neighbor); low capital, opens health funders.
- **Aging (medium):** an older-women track in PSH; small pool, strong narrative.
- **Families / maternal (far, not recommended):** new population, licensing, mission change.

### Caveats
Tagged dollars understate what funders would give (general operating excluded); distance ratings are judgment; federal notices are a snapshot.

### Confidence
Medium.

## M9 need and capacity context

Script `scripts/09_m9_need_capacity.py`. Charts `charts/m9_*.png`; tables `chart_data/m9_*.csv`. Insights M9-01, M9-02.

### Question
How deep is the need in Calvary's service area, how is DC's homeless population moving, and how much of the system's capacity for single women does Calvary now provide?

### Method
- ACS 2020–24 five-year estimates by ward from `dim_geo` (DC wards are Census state-legislative-district geographies; 90% margins of error in the table).
- HUD point-in-time counts for CoC DC-500 from `supp_homeless_counts` (2007–2025).
- HUD Housing Inventory Count 2022–2025 from `supp_hic_projects`: Calvary's TH, PSH and RRH beds, and its TH beds as a share of all DC transitional-housing beds; women-focused providers flagged in the table.
- Ward map from DC Open Data ward boundaries (`raw/geo`), colored by ACS poverty rate, with Calvary's site.

### Findings
| Indicator (ACS 2020–24) | Ward 7 | Ward 8 | DC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Poverty rate | 22.9% | 30.6% | 15.4% |
| Female poverty rate | 24.8% | 31.7% | 16.3% |
| Renters paying 30%+ of income | 55.3% | 54.6% | 46.6% |
| Renters paying 50%+ | 33.3% | 32.5% | 23.6% |
| Unemployment | 12.7% | 13.4% | 6.3% |
| Female householder, no spouse | 29.0% | 29.8% | 13.1% |

1. **Need** (M9-01): Ward 8 has twice the city's poverty rate and the highest female poverty in DC; a third of renters in both wards pay more than half their income in rent; unemployment is double the city rate.
2. **System trend** (M9-02): DC's homeless count fell from 8,350 (2016) to 5,138 (2025), with a post-pandemic rebound in 2023–24. The system is shrinking while per-person investment (PSH, vouchers) rises.
3. **Calvary's capacity**: 124 beds across transitional, permanent supportive and rapid-rehousing programs in 2025 (94 TH, 16 PSH at Sister Circle, 14 RRH), up from 68 in 2022 (45 TH, 16 PSH, 7 RRH). Its 94 transitional beds are 6.8% of the District's, up from 2.5% (45 beds) in 2022. Sisters Rise PSH (24 units) appears in 2024 only. Among women-focused providers in the HIC (N Street Village 457, House of Ruth 388, Open Arms 412, New Endeavors 135, Calvary 124 beds in 2025), Calvary is the fastest-growing.

### Charts
`m9_01_ward_indicators`, `m9_02_dc_pit`, `m9_03_calvary_hic_share`, `m9_05_ward_map` (if boundaries loaded; see analysis log); tables `m9_04_women_focused_beds.csv`.

### Caveats
- Ward-level ACS has wide margins of error for small subgroups; tract-level figures were not used.
- HIC counts beds, not people served, and HIC project naming changes year to year (Calvary's projects were re-labelled in 2024).
- PIT gender breakdowns are not in HUD's PIT workbook; the CoC's own 2024 subpopulation table counts 2,167 women among 5,616 people.

### Confidence
High.

## M10 named-comparator profiles (Calvary CEO request)

Script `scripts/10_m10_profiles.py`. Tables `chart_data/m10_01…m10_05`; charts `m10_01_comparator_trajectories`, `m10_02_dwc_federal_programs`. Insights M10-01, M10-02. Both organizations appear as reference rows on every peer chart (M3, M6).

### Downtown Women's Center (DWC), Los Angeles — EIN 31-1597223, NTEE P83, FY = calendar year

| | FY2014 | FY2018 | FY2021 | FY2024 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $6.3M | $11.6M | $21.0M | $34.4M |
| Government share (line 1e) | 24% | 31% | 44% | 57% |
| Private contributions | $4.0M | $6.9M | $9.9M | $12.8M |
| Program service revenue | $0.5M | $1.1M | $1.2M | $1.8M |
| Months of cash | 2.1 | 3.1 | 3.1 | 2.4 |

- **Trajectory:** revenue grew 5.5x since FY2014 ($6.3M to $34.4M) and 3x since FY2018 ($11.6M); government went from a quarter to well over half. Private contributions tripled in absolute terms but fell from 64% to 37% of revenue. Program service revenue (social enterprise, rental) is 5%.
- **Federal money** ($21.6M FY2020–25 in single audits): 99% pass-through, led by HUD CoC 14.267 ($14.3M), ESG 14.231 ($3.5M), VOCA 16.575 ($2.7M), Coronavirus Relief Fund, SNAP E&T, CDBG, EFSP, plus a $194K HUD Community Project Funding award. These are the same federal channels Calvary uses, at about five times the scale, routed through LA County and LAHSA rather than TCP.
- **Programs:** 159 PSH units plus community-based housing (451 people housed in 2024); Skid Row's only women's health clinic (with JWCH); MADE by DWC paid transitional work; Rosa's Place (97 PSH units) under construction. 358 employees, 1,750 volunteers.
- **Funders:** 2023 donor list 202 organizations, 2025 list 148; $1M+ band includes GO-Biz, LA County DHS and LAHSA; announced grants: Hilton $1.53M over two years (2026), Blue Shield of California Foundation $450K (2024), Ahmanson $325K (FY2023), Anthem Blue Cross Foundation $200K (2023) and $300K (2026), LA County First District $3M (2025). DMV funders in the data: Bank of America Charitable Foundation ($154K over four years), Wells Fargo ($100K), Give Lively, ImpactAssets, Bainum, JPMorgan Chase. DAF grants to DWC are not captured (Schedule I kept for DC/MD/VA recipients).
- **What transfers to Calvary:** (1) the housing-development pipeline, using CoC and county PSH money to own and operate units; (2) the health-clinic partnership model with a community health provider; (3) a paid transitional-work enterprise (MADE) as a workforce program with earned revenue; (4) the scale of its donor base (hundreds of institutional names, big corporate health funders). What does not transfer: the mix. DWC scaled *with* government and runs on 2–3 months of cash, which is the exposure Calvary is trying to reduce.

### California Black Women's Collective Empowerment Institute (runs SheWorks) — EIN 88-2046704, Carson CA, FYE June, founded 2022

| | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $1.38M | $1.49M | $1.84M |
| Government share | 88% | 85% | 70% |
| Private contributions | $169K | $223K | $558K |
| Months of cash | 28.5 | 4.8 | 8.2 |

- A young research-and-advocacy institute (Black Women's Think Tank / Research and Innovation Institute, Conversations for Black Women, Protecting Black Women and Girls) that started almost entirely on government funding and is diversifying quickly; it also makes small grants ($42.5K to 8 organizations in TY2024).
- **SheWorks** was announced in October 2025 and runs its first cohort (about 30 women, January–May 2026) at the L.A. Care / Blue Shield Promise Community Resource Center in Long Beach, with stipends, childcare and ride credits; the LA County Federation of Labor is a partial funder and the health plans host in kind. No FAC or USAspending awards. Its funding will appear only in TY2025+ filings.
- **What transfers to Calvary:** the program design (cohort model, stipends, childcare and transport, employer and health-plan partners, system-impacted women as a named population) as an upgrade to Step Up DC; the partner structure (labor federation + health plans) as a corporate-partnership pattern. Not a funding model to copy: the parent relies more on government than Calvary does.

### Caveats
DWC's fiscal year is the calendar year; line 1e is the government measure for both (no audits in the data except DWC's single audits for federal money); LA-area funders of DWC are only partly captured (web lists without amounts, DMV funders' filings only).

### Confidence
High on DWC's trajectory and federal programs; medium on funder lists; medium on the SheWorks parent (three filings, program launched after the last one).

## The verdict

From `recommendations/funding_pressure_verdict.md`; the full evidence table is there.

Calvary is under **real funding pressure, but not because its government share is unusual**. Government supplies 53% of revenue (FY2022–24 average on the audit basis; 58% in FY25 on the 990), which is mid-pack among DC peers (11th of 19) and at the 57th percentile among DC human-services organizations that report government revenue; against all filers (no government line counted as 0%) Calvary is in the top quarter (84th in DC, 74th nationally). The pressure is structural: (1) the government money arrives through **three channels, two of them via a single intermediary** (TCP carries the HUD CoC renewals and the DHS contract, about three-quarters of Calvary's recurring award base: 78% of the $4.1M 2024 award base, chart m2_01); (2) **private revenue is flat and concentrated**: filed institutional grants have stayed near $1M a year from the same 26–29 funders, and one funder (GWCF, including the time-limited Health Equity Fund) is 27% of five years of filed grants, while event receipts held near $0.53–0.60M (FY24 $596K, FY25 $533K; the FY25 990 presented gala receipts as fundraising-event income, line 8a with $259K of direct costs netted, instead of contributions, line 1c); (3) **FY25 ran a deficit**: −$607K, with cash at 4.4 months of expenses (7.5 in FY21), and at the FY25 run-rate cash lasts about 41 months with no shock at all. The DC budget lines behind Calvary's local money are flat to rising through FY2027, but the Mayor proposed cuts to victim-services and DV lines in each of the last two springs and the Council restored them; the FY2027 OVSJG restoration is $5.1M one-time plus $0.5M recurring, so the FY2028 base is in play again. The local risk is annual and political, not structural. The federal side is the larger uncertainty: the FY2025 CoC NOFO was enjoined and FY2025 renewals were paid in full, so the live question is the FY2026 CoC NOFO (protected renewals 60% of demand, a $1.3B transitional-housing and services set-aside, applications closed 30 September 2026, awards expected about December 2026, litigation pending), and HUD's 29 September 2026 notice ends the EHV program (families leased on 30 September 2026 convert to non-reissuable tenant-protection vouchers by 31 December 2026, so Sisters Rise's voucher base cannot be rebuilt). Both point the same way: the TCP channel is the cloud.

**Rating: moderate-to-high pressure, driven by channel concentration and liquidity rather than by the government share.**

**What would change the verdict**

- Calvary's FY24 and FY25 audits and its TCP subgrant agreements: they settle the ceilings-vs-recognized gap (D1) and the Sisters Rise question (D2). The audited FY22–23 single audits already place the gap in the CoC stream, so reconcile CoC draw-down first, then DHS. If awards are being under-drawn, the first recommendation becomes "draw what is awarded".
- Flag D3 (event income) is closed, resolved from the 990 itself: receipts held near $0.53–0.60M and the FY25 change was one of presentation, so the private trend is flat rather than falling.
- A change in the core-peer set (provisional) would move the rank (swapping three provisional peers moves Calvary from 11th to 12th of 19) but not the sector percentile.
